note: Every factual claim the app makes about health, cost, climate or animals points at one of these. Each entry records what kind of evidence it is, because a randomized trial and a modeling study do not deserve the same confidence, and an app that flattens that difference is misleading people politely. 'checked' is the date a human or agent last confirmed the bibliographic details against the source or its publisher listing.

evidenceLevels.rct: Randomized controlled trial — the strongest single-study design for cause and effect.
evidenceLevels.meta-analysis: Systematic review pooling many studies. Strength depends on what was pooled.
evidenceLevels.cohort: Observational follow-up of a population. Shows association; cannot prove cause on its own.
evidenceLevels.modeling: A model built on other data. Useful for scale and direction, not precision.
evidenceLevels.guideline: Consensus guidance from a professional body, weighing the whole evidence base.
evidenceLevels.regulatory: An official standard or authorised claim.
evidenceLevels.dataset: Compiled statistics from an official or well-documented source.

sources.authors: Poore, J. & Nemecek, T.
sources.title: Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers
sources.summary: Consolidated data from ~38,700 commercially viable farms across 119 countries and 40 products, covering five environmental indicators.
sources.caveat: A meta-analysis of life-cycle assessments, not an experiment. Variation between farms producing the same food is large — the highest-impact producers of a plant food can exceed the lowest-impact producers of an animal food.

sources.authors: Crippa, M., Solazzo, E., Guizzardi, D., Monforti-Ferrario, F., Tubiello, F. N. & Leip, A.
sources.title: Food systems are responsible for a third of global anthropogenic GHG emissions
sources.summary: Estimated food-system emissions at 18 Gt CO2-equivalent per year in 2015, about 34% of the global total.
sources.caveat: Uses a broader system boundary than Poore & Nemecek, which is why its share is higher. The IPCC's own range for food-system emissions is 21–37%.

sources.authors: Springmann, M., Clark, M. A., Rayner, M., Scarborough, P. & Webb, P.
sources.title: The global and regional costs of healthy and sustainable dietary patterns: a modelling study
sources.summary: Compared the cost of seven sustainable dietary patterns with current diets in 150 countries, using World Bank International Comparison Program food prices. In high-income countries vegan diets cost 21–34% less, vegetarian 27–31% less, and low-meat flexitarian about 14% less than the current typical diet.
sources.caveat: Models retail food costs only. It does not price time, cooking skill, kitchen equipment, or the reality that the cheapest option is not available in every neighborhood.

sources.authors: Estruch, R., Ros, E., Salas-Salvadó, J., et al.
sources.title: Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts
sources.summary: 7,447 adults at high cardiovascular risk, randomized to a Mediterranean diet with extra-virgin olive oil, the same diet with nuts, or a low-fat control. Roughly a 30% lower rate of heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death over a median 4.8 years.
sources.caveat: The 2013 publication was retracted and republished in 2018 after irregularities in randomization at some sites; the reanalysis, which is the version cited here, reached materially the same conclusions. Participants were older Spanish adults already at high risk, so the size of the effect may not transfer to everyone.

sources.authors: Sacks, F. M., Lichtenstein, A. H., Wu, J. H. Y., et al.
sources.title: Dietary fats and cardiovascular disease: a presidential advisory from the American Heart Association
sources.summary: Randomized trials that lowered saturated fat and replaced it with polyunsaturated vegetable oil reduced cardiovascular disease by about 30% — an effect the advisory notes is similar in size to statin treatment.
sources.caveat: The benefit comes from the replacement. Cutting saturated fat and replacing it with refined starch or sugar does not show the same effect.

sources.authors: Reynolds, A., Mann, J., Cummings, J., Winter, N., Mete, E. & Te Morenga, L.
sources.title: Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
sources.summary: 185 prospective studies and 58 clinical trials. People eating the most dietary fiber had 15–30% lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality than those eating the least, with the clearest benefit between 25 g and 30 g a day.
sources.caveat: The mortality findings are observational — people who eat more fiber differ in other ways. The trial data within the review support the blood-pressure and cholesterol effects more directly.

sources.authors: Neal, B., Wu, Y., Feng, X., et al.
sources.title: Effect of salt substitution on cardiovascular events and death
sources.summary: 20,995 people in 600 Chinese villages, randomized to a 75% sodium chloride / 25% potassium chloride salt substitute or regular salt. Stroke fell about 14%, major cardiovascular events about 13%, and death from any cause about 12% over roughly five years.
sources.caveat: Participants had had a stroke or were over 60 with high blood pressure, in a setting where most salt is added during home cooking. Potassium-based substitutes are not safe for everyone — people with kidney disease or on certain blood-pressure drugs should ask a clinician first.

sources.authors: Grundy, S. M., Stone, N. J., Bailey, A. L., et al.
sources.title: 2018 AHA/ACC/Multisociety guideline on the management of blood cholesterol
sources.summary: The consensus US guideline on cholesterol management. Treats a heart-healthy dietary pattern as the foundation of care for everyone, and drug therapy as necessary on top of it for defined risk groups.
sources.caveat: A guideline, not a study. It is the considered summary of a large evidence base, and it is periodically revised.

sources.authors: National Lipid Association
sources.title: Update on familial hypercholesterolemia: an expert clinical consensus
sources.summary: In familial hypercholesterolaemia — an inherited condition causing lifelong high LDL cholesterol — lifestyle change is an adjunct to drug therapy and is unlikely to reach treatment targets on its own.
sources.caveat: Specific to an inherited condition affecting roughly 1 in 250 people. It is cited here for one purpose: to be straight about the limits of diet.

sources.authors: US Food and Drug Administration
sources.title: Health claims: soluble fiber from certain foods and risk of coronary heart disease
sources.summary: The FDA permits foods to claim a coronary-heart-disease benefit for beta-glucan soluble fiber from oats and barley at a daily intake of 3 g, alongside a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol.
sources.caveat: An authorised claim about a food component, not a promise about any one person's outcome.

sources.authors: Our World in Data, from FAOSTAT
sources.title: Land animals slaughtered for meat
sources.publication: Our World in Data / UN FAO
sources.summary: More than 80 billion land animals were slaughtered for meat globally in 2022 — the large majority of them chickens.
sources.caveat: Counts animals slaughtered for meat. It excludes fish and other aquatic animals, which are counted in tonnes rather than individuals, and excludes deaths in egg and dairy production.

sources.authors: US Departments of Agriculture and Health and Human Services
sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025
sources.summary: The federal dietary guidance, including the estimated calorie needs by age, sex and activity level used for children's portions in this app, and the sodium limits used by age band.
sources.caveat: Population-level guidance. It describes averages, not any individual's requirement.

sources.authors: US Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service
sources.title: FoodData Central
sources.detail: Foundation Foods, SR Legacy and FNDDS
sources.summary: The public-domain nutrient database every ingredient value in this app is derived from.
sources.caveat: Values are representative averages. Real foods vary by variety, season, soil and brand — and packaged items vary enormously between brands.

sources.authors: Mifflin, M. D., St Jeor, S. T., Hill, L. A., Scott, B. J., Daugherty, S. A. & Koh, Y. O.
sources.title: A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals
sources.summary: The equation this app uses to estimate adult daily energy needs.
sources.caveat: A prediction from height, weight, age and sex. For an individual it is typically within about 10% — useful for sizing a pot of food, not for anything medical.

sources.authors: McDonald, D. et al.
sources.title: American Gut: an Open Platform for Citizen Science Microbiome Research
sources.summary: Self-reported diet and gut microbiome sequencing from more than 10,000 volunteers. People reporting more than 30 different plant foods a week carried more diverse gut bacterial communities than those reporting 10 or fewer.
sources.caveat: An observational study of a self-selected, largely Western and health-interested volunteer cohort, with diet recorded by self-report. It shows an association between plant variety and microbiome diversity; it does not show that reaching a count of thirty causes better health, and greater microbiome diversity is not itself a clinical outcome.

sources.authors: Shukla, A. P., Iliescu, R. G., Thomas, C. E. & Aronne, L. J.
sources.title: Food order has a significant impact on postprandial glucose and insulin levels
sources.summary: A randomized crossover trial in 11 adults with type 2 diabetes. The same 628-kcal meal was eaten on two days a week apart, once with carbohydrate first and once with vegetables and protein first. Eating the carbohydrate last lowered post-meal glucose by about 29% at 30 minutes, 37% at 60 and 17% at 120, with lower insulin at 60 and 120 minutes.
sources.caveat: Eleven participants, two meals, glucose measured for two hours. It shows that meal order changes the post-meal glucose curve; it does not show a long-term health outcome, and the effect depends on the parts of the meal actually being eaten separately.

sources.authors: Buffey, A. J., Herring, M. P., Langley, C. K., Donnelly, A. E. & Carson, B. P.
sources.title: The acute effects of interrupting prolonged sitting time in adults with standing and light-intensity walking on biomarkers of cardiometabolic health in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.summary: Pooled seven studies comparing prolonged sitting with the same sitting broken up by standing or by short bouts of light-intensity walking. Light walking lowered post-meal glucose and insulin significantly; standing alone did much less.
sources.caveat: Acute studies measuring the hours after a meal, in small samples, mostly in healthy or overweight adults. It supports a short walk as a cheap habit, not as a treatment for anything.

sources.authors: Katz, P. O., Dunbar, K. B., Schnoll-Sussman, F. H., Greer, K. B., Yadlapati, R. & Spechler, S. J.
sources.title: ACG clinical guideline for the diagnosis and management of gastroesophageal reflux disease
sources.summary: The American College of Gastroenterology's guidance on reflux disease. Among its lifestyle recommendations: avoid meals within two to three hours of lying down, and raise the head of the bed for people with nighttime symptoms.
sources.caveat: Guidance for people who have reflux symptoms. It is not general advice about when everybody should eat dinner.

sources.authors: Robinson, E., Almiron-Roig, E., Rutters, F., de Graaf, C., Forde, C. G., Tudur Smith, C., Nevitt, S. J. & Jebb, S. A.
sources.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis examining the effect of eating rate on energy intake and hunger
sources.publication: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
sources.summary: Pooled experiments in which the same meal was eaten quickly or slowly. Eating more slowly reduced how much was eaten at that meal, with no increase in hunger reported afterward.
sources.caveat: Single-meal laboratory studies of intake, not trials of long-term eating or health. It describes how a meal feels and how much of it gets eaten, nothing more.

sources.authors: Institute of Medicine, Panel on Dietary Reference Intakes for Electrolytes and Water
sources.title: Dietary Reference Intakes for water, potassium, sodium, chloride, and sulfate
sources.summary: Sets an adequate intake for total water of about 3.7 liters a day for men and 2.7 for women, counting all beverages and the water in food. Roughly 20% of total water comes from food.
sources.caveat: An adequate intake is the median of what apparently well-hydrated people consume, not a target anybody has to reach. Needs vary with climate, activity and health, and some conditions come with fluid limits set by a clinician.

sources.authors: US Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR program
sources.title: Dishwashers: product specification and savings
sources.summary: Certified standard-size dishwashers use 3.2 gallons of water per cycle or less, against a federal maximum of 5.0 gallons, and the program compares this with up to 27 gallons for washing the same load by hand.
sources.caveat: The 27-gallon hand-washing figure assumes a running tap. Washing efficiently in a filled basin uses far less than that and closes most of the gap. The dishwasher advantage also depends on running full loads and skipping the pre-rinse.

sources.authors: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D. & Bjork, R.
sources.title: Learning styles: concepts and evidence
sources.publication: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
sources.summary: Reviewed the evidence for the meshing hypothesis — that teaching matched to a learner's self-reported style improves outcomes. Found almost no studies using the experimental design capable of testing it, and the few that did produced results contradicting the hypothesis.
sources.caveat: A review of study designs rather than a single experiment. It does not claim people have no preferences; it claims that matching instruction to a stated preference has not been shown to help, which is a narrower and better-supported point.

sources.authors: Clark, J. M. & Paivio, A.
sources.title: Dual coding theory and education
sources.summary: Sets out the case that verbal and visual information are processed by separate but connected systems, so material encoded both ways is retrieved more reliably than material encoded either way alone.
sources.caveat: A theoretical review with supporting studies, largely from laboratory learning tasks rather than kitchens. The effect is about presenting both channels to everyone, not about matching a channel to a person.

sources.authors: Mayer, R. E. & Moreno, R.
sources.title: Nine ways to reduce cognitive load in multimedia learning
sources.summary: Summarizes experiments on presenting words and pictures together, including that related words and images help most when placed near each other, and that adding redundant material can hurt rather than help.
sources.caveat: Drawn from short instructional multimedia experiments with students. The direction of the findings is well replicated; the sizes are specific to those materials.

sources.authors: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P. & Sweller, J.
sources.title: The expertise reversal effect
sources.summary: Instructional support that measurably helps beginners becomes useless and then actively harmful as the learner gains experience, because processing the scaffolding costs effort the expert no longer needs to spend.
sources.caveat: Established across several domains in controlled instruction studies. It describes a difference that changes with experience, not a fixed trait of a person.
